A reign is the period of time during which a king, queen, emperor, empress, or any supreme ruler holds power. It is the entire stretch of their time in authority — from the moment they take the throne to the moment they leave it, whether through death, removal from power, or voluntary stepping down.

Think of it as an era defined by who is in charge at the very top.
Simple examples in the primary sense

"Queen Victoria's reign lasted 63 years."
→ Victoria was the ruling queen of Britain for 63 years.

"The reign of Emperor Augustus brought stability to Rome."
→ During the time Augustus was emperor, Rome was relatively stable.

"His reign ended when he was overthrown."
→ His time as supreme ruler came to a close when people removed him from power.

A reign isn't just a count of years on a throne. It encompasses everything that happened during that period — the wars, the achievements, the failures, the laws made, the culture of the time. This is why historians place events "during the reign of" a particular ruler: they are giving you the context of who held ultimate authority when those events occurred.

So when someone says "this happened during the reign of King Henry VIII," they mean both when it happened and under whose supreme authority it happened. The two ideas are bundled together in one word.
The figurative meaning (beyond kings and queens)

Reign is not limited to royalty. It is widely used to describe any period in which a person, a force, an idea, or an entity is completely dominant in its domain.

"During his reign as CEO, the company became the world's largest."
→ The period during which he was the top authority, and the company thrived under him.

"Scientists say the dinosaurs' reign on Earth lasted over 160 million years."
→ The long era during which dinosaurs were the dominant creatures on the planet.

"After decades of dominance, the champion's reign finally came to an end."
→ The period during which that champion was supreme in their sport.

In these figurative uses, reign communicates something stronger than just "time" or "era." It implies supremacy — the subject isn't merely present during that period, it dominates it completely.
The emotional weight and connotation of the word

This is a subtle but important point. Reign carries a sense of grandeur and significance. It suggests authority that is absolute, or close to it. This is precisely why writers and speakers choose it over neutral alternatives like "time," "period," or "era" — those words are flat and descriptive. Reign tells you that whoever or whatever is being described stood at the very top, unchallenged, during that stretch of time.

This also means the word can be used ironically or negatively to describe something undesirable that dominated a period: "the reign of chaos," "the reign of mediocrity." Here, the word isn't praising what reigned — it's dramatizing just how thoroughly that thing dominated.

Reign of terror — A period defined by extreme violence, fear, and brutality inflicted upon people. It is most famously used to describe a violent phase of the French Revolution (1793–94), but it is applied broadly whenever a situation is thoroughly defined by fear and suffering.

Reign supreme — To be the most powerful, dominant, or successful in a particular area. "In the 1990s, grunge music reigned supreme." (Note: this uses the verb form of reign, but the meaning is the same — to occupy the position of supreme dominance.)

A long reign / a short reign — Plain descriptions of the duration of someone's time at the top.
Don't confuse reign with these two words

Because "reign," "rein," and "rain" are all pronounced identically, mixing them up in writing is one of the most common mistakes in English. Here is the clear distinction:

Rein is the strap or cord used to guide and control a horse. Figuratively, "to rein something in" means to restrain or limit it ("the government tried to rein in spending"), and "free rein" means the freedom to act as one chooses ("she was given free rein to redesign the office").

Rain is water falling from the sky as precipitation.

Reign alone carries the meaning of ruling, supreme authority, and the period of that authority.

A useful memory trick: reign contains the word king hiding inside it if you look — it has a "g" that hints at royalty, and is the only one of the three that has anything to do with power.

Reign, as a noun, is the period during which someone or something holds supreme power or dominance. It always has a beginning and an end. It applies literally to monarchs and rulers, and figuratively to any person, force, creature, or idea that stands at the top of its domain for a stretch of time. The word carries weight — it signals that the authority in question was not ordinary or partial, but supreme and defining of its era.
